facts.statement: Thecachampsa possessed a long, slender snout similar to that of living gharials.
facts.quote: Like living gharials, it had a long, slender snout.

facts.statement: The teeth of Thecachampsa were long and recurved.
facts.quote: The teeth were long and recurved.

facts.statement: Unlike its living relatives, Thecachampsa was a marine animal that inhabited estuaries and shallow coastal waters.
facts.quote: Unlike its living relatives, Thecachampsa was marine, inhabiting estuaries and shallow coastal waters.

facts.statement: American paleontologist Joseph Leidy described the species Crocodylus antiquus in 1852 from Miocene deposits in Virginia.
facts.quote: In 1852, American paleontologist Joseph Leidy described Crocodylus antiquus from Miocene deposits in the Lee family's ancestral home in Virginia.

facts.statement: The holotype for the species described by Leidy was a tooth found in the Calvert Formation of Virginia.
facts.quote: The holotype was a tooth found in the Calvert Formation of Virginia.

facts.statement: The genus Thecachampsa was erected by Edward Drinker Cope in 1867, originally containing two species based on teeth without a designated type species.
facts.quote: The new genus Thecachampsa was erected by Edward Drinker Cope in 1867, containing two species, T. sericodon and T. contusor, both also based on teeth, but no type species was designated.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope designated T. sericodon as the type species for Thecachampsa in 1882.
facts.quote: Cope (1882) designated T. sericodon as the Thecachampsa type species.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named the species T. sicaria in 1869 based on a jaw fragment and a dorsal vertebra.
facts.quote: In 1869, Cope named a fourth species, T. sicaria, from a jaw fragment and a dorsal vertebra.

facts.statement: The teeth of T. sicaria were lenticular in cross-section with sharp cutting edges, distinguishing them from other species.
facts.quote: Unlike those of other species, the teeth of T. sicaria were lenticular (lens-shaped) in cross section with sharp cutting edges.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named T. fastigiata in 1870 as a reassignment of a species originally named by Leidy in 1852.
facts.quote: Cope named a new species, T. fastigiata, in 1870 as a reassignment of Crocodylus fastigiatus, named by Leidy in 1852.

facts.statement: Species within Thecachampsa were primarily distinguished by differences in tooth shape, which was the most common fossil material found.
facts.quote: These species were distinguished from one another primarily by differences in the shape of the teeth, the most common material found.

facts.statement: The genus Thecachampsa was synonymized with Crocodylus in 1973 but is now considered a valid genus.
facts.quote: The genus was synonymized with Crocodylus in 1973, but has since been regarded as valid.

facts.statement: In 2001, A.C. Myrick synonymized Gavialosuchus americanus with T. antiqua.
facts.quote: In 2001, A.C. Myrick synonymized Gavialosuchus americanus, another "tomistomine" from the eastern United States, with T. antiqua.

facts.statement: A younger species was first described as Tomistoma americanus in 1915 from Florida, with remains found in formations across New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina.
facts.quote: A geologically younger species was first described from Florida as Tomistoma americanus in 1915, with remains having been found from the Kirkwood Formation in New Jersey, the Calvert Formation in Maryland, the Chesapeake Group of Virginia, and the Pungo River and Yorktown Formations of North Carolina.

facts.statement: Fossils of Thecachampsa range in age from the late Early Miocene to the early Pliocene.
facts.quote: Fossils of the species are present in deposits that range in age from the late Early Miocene to the early Pliocene.

facts.statement: Remains of Thecachampsa have been found in Florida, California, Baja California, and Costa Rica.
facts.quote: Remains have also been found from Florida, California, Baja California, and, more recently, Costa Rica.

facts.statement: Thecachampsa belongs to the parent group Gavialoidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Gavialoidea

facts.statement: Thecachampsa is classified within the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The time range for Thecachampsa is from the Thanetian to the Late Pleistocene, approximately 59.24 to 0.014 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Thanetian to Late Pleistocene (59.24 to 0.014 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are 39 recorded fossil occurrences of Thecachampsa in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 39

facts.statement: Some studies have placed North American forms within Gavialosuchus, but most analyses show a broad phylogenetic separation between these forms and Gavialosuchus eggenburgensis.
facts.quote: A few studies such as that of Jouve et al. (2008) have kept the species within Gavialosuchus, leaving T. antiqua as the only species within Thecachampsa, though they didn't test Thecachampsa antiqua in their phylogenetic analysis, and most other analyses recover a clade including all North American forms that had previously been referred Gavialosuchus with a broad phylogenetic separation between them and G. eggenburgensis.

facts.statement: It is debated whether different tooth shapes represent distinct species or variations within a single species, as complete skulls showing these variations were previously referred to Gavialosuchus.
facts.quote: The different tooth shapes that distinguished the species were considered variations in the dentition of a single species. However, the variation in dentition could only be seen in complete skulls, all of which had been referred to Gavialosuchus before the genus was synonymized with Thecachampsa.

facts.statement: Most subsequent analyses reject the suggestion that T. americana and T. sericodon are the same species, citing clear differences between T. americana and T. antiqua.
facts.quote: Most subsequent analyses have not accepted these suggestions based on clear differences between T. americana and T. antiqua and the lack of differences not explained by taphonomy between T. antiqua and T. sericodon.
